newsitem.title: SPAIN: Matador issues at record high, market seen slowing.
newsitem.headline: Matador issues at record high, market seen slowing.

text.p: Matador bond issues, which have soared to record high volumes in the first five months of the year, are expected to slow in the coming months, dealers said.
From January to May 1997, matador issues reached levels equal to two thirds of that recorded for the whole of 1996.
New issues of peseta bonds totalled 610 billion pesetas, out of which 235 billion pesetas were in equity-linked bonds while the remaining 375 billion pesetas were fixed-income products.
Despite the favourable comparison with a record number of issues for the whole of 1996 of 923 billion, dealers said the Matador primary market was now likely to take a rest.
"It's clearly a market where at the moment customers have less demand than three months ago," said Grant Ashton, executive director at interbank trading at UBS in London.
Yields at record lows and a new law allowing funds to make direct use of derivatives are seen as the key reasons behind a possible slowing in activity.
"People are wary to do anything because...yields are at all time lows," said Ashton.
UBS, which says it is the biggest player in the Matador secondary market, expects to see activity picking up when the market falls.
"People are buying on dips," Asthon added.

The new derivative tools which can now be used by domestic investment trusts will reduce their demand for matadors, analysts said. Investment trusts were one of the main clients for equity-linked matadors at the beginning of the year.
"Investment trusts who need to provide a minimum level of yield for their clients, were using these equity-linked issues as a way to cover themselves," said a dealer in Madrid.
"But now investment trusts are less innovative, in the sense that they are launching fewer new products and new rules give them more alternatives," he added.
In the first quarter of this year, many of these equity-linked matadors were intended to guarantee subscribers a minimum level of yield, an important feature for investment trusts.
"The first semester of this year was very busy, but I expect the second part of the year to be less so," the trader said.
He forecast the total number of new Matadors to be around 300 to 400 billion pesetas in the remaining part of the year which would bring the total number of issues for 1997 close to 1996 levels.
But other dealers were less convinced of a possible slowing down in the market.

At Banco Santander de Negocio, which leads the Matador primary market with a market share of around 31 percent, Luis Ordonez responsible for new issues said: "It seems that structured new issues are slowing down."
But he added that ,as is the case for government debt, the future will depend on Europe's monetary union.
He said the oulook for matadors would also be tied to public debt, as in the last two years.

Government debt has enjoyed a bull market since 1996, with the 10-year spread over Bunds falling from 330 basis points in March 1996 to 100 basis points at the start of 1997 and to around 60 bps currently.
